details:
**"Starving Time"**
The catastrophic winter of 1609–1610, when Jamestown's population fell from roughly 500 to about 60 amid famine, disease, and a Powhatan siege. Colonists ate horses, rats, and shoe leather, and there is evidence of cannibalism; survivors included Temperance Flowerdew.

**John Rolfe and tobacco**
Rolfe introduced a sweeter strain of tobacco, grown from seeds obtained from the Spanish Caribbean, around 1612. Tobacco became the colony's cash crop and made Virginia economically viable.

**John Smith and Pocahontas**
Smith was an early leader of Jamestown who, according to his own later account, was captured by the Powhatans and saved from execution by Pocahontas, daughter of Chief Powhatan. He imposed the rule "he that will not work shall not eat" before returning to England in 1609 after a gunpowder injury.

**Bacon's Rebellion (1676)**
An uprising led by Nathaniel Bacon against Governor William Berkeley, who had refused to authorize a militia commission to fight Native Americans. It began after a dispute with the Doeg people over Thomas Mathews's plantation, saw attacks on Native groups including the Pamunkey, and ended with Bacon's forces burning Jamestown before Bacon died of dysentery.

**Opechancanough and the 1622 massacre**
The brother and eventual successor of Chief Powhatan, who once captured John Smith on a hunting trip. He led the 1622 surprise attack that killed about a third of the colonists, including at Martin's Hundred, and a later 1644 attack; he was shot in the back by a guard while a prisoner and was succeeded by Necotowance.

**Lord De La Warr**
Thomas West, Baron De La Warr, the colony's governor, arrived with relief ships and supplies in June 1610 just as the starving survivors were abandoning the settlement. His arrival saved Jamestown and launched the First Anglo-Powhatan War.

**Sea Venture and the Third Supply**
The flagship of the 1609 Third Supply mission, which was wrecked on Bermuda in a hurricane. The loss of its supplies and leaders worsened the Starving Time, and the wreck is thought to have inspired Shakespeare's The Tempest.

**Susan Constant, Godspeed, and Discovery**
The three ships, commanded by Christopher Newport, that brought the first colonists to Jamestown in 1607. Newport later returned with supply missions.

**Triangular fort**
The original James Fort, built in 1607 as a triangle of wooden palisade walls with bulwarks at each corner. It is the source of clues calling Jamestown a "triangle-shaped colony."

**Werowocomoco and the Powhatan Confederacy**
Werowocomoco was the capital of Chief Powhatan, across the York River area from Jamestown, and a hub for trading English copper and beads for food. Pocahontas, also called Matoaka, came from there and later took the name Rebecca when she married John Rolfe.

**House of Burgesses**
The first elected legislative assembly in English America, which first met at Jamestown in 1619 under Governor George Yeardley. That same year, enslaved Africans, including a woman named Angela, arrived at Point Comfort.

**Edward Maria Wingfield and Bartholomew Gosnold**
Wingfield was the first president of the colony's council and chose the settlement's site, but he was deposed in 1607 amid accusations including atheism. Gosnold, a key organizer of the expedition, died at Jamestown that same year.

**Thomas Dale and the "Lawes Divine, Morall and Martiall"**
Dale, a deputy governor, imposed this harsh martial-law code around 1611 to restore discipline. He also founded the upriver settlement of Henricus to grow food.

**Chanco's warning to Richard Pace**
Chanco, a Powhatan boy living with colonist Richard Pace, warned him of the planned 1622 attack. Pace alerted Jamestown in time to save it, though outlying settlements like Martin's Hundred were devastated.

**George Percy**
A colonist who led Jamestown during the Starving Time and wrote an account of its horrors. He also recorded a 1610 raid in which his soldiers killed the children of a Paspahegh chief by throwing them into the water and shooting them.
